vignette:
He is a 63-year-old Oceania man who has spent much of his adult life organizing neighborhood meetings, mediating disputes, and helping people find their voices in local politics. He speaks about his work with a quiet pride, as something that has given shape to his life after divorce and the gradual narrowing of his world that followed. Before the accident, he describes himself as steady and dependable, the kind of person others called when something needed sorting out. He was used to being the one who stayed calm.

The accident happens on a wet afternoon while he is driving home from a community forum. He remembers the road shining with rain, the blur of headlights, and then the sudden impact of another vehicle crossing into his lane. For an instant he is sure he is dying. The force throws him forward, then everything goes strangely still except for the sound of the engine and his own breathing. He is trapped, pinned in the car, and the certainty that he may not get out becomes the central memory of that day. Later he will say that what frightens him most is not only the pain, but the helplessness of knowing his body cannot respond fast enough to save him.

In the weeks after, he is physically injured and exhausted, but it is the shift in his inner life that unsettles him most. He startsle sharply at sudden noises, especially brakes, metal bangs, and rain striking the windshield. Driving becomes tense and effortful. He grips the steering wheel hard, scans intersections repeatedly, and chooses longer routes to avoid places where traffic merges quickly. At times he sits in the car after parking, unable to move inside the familiar space that now feels unsafe. He notices that his chest tightens before he even realizes what has set him off.

He begins waking in the night with his heart racing, often after dreams he cannot fully remember but that leave him with a sense of being trapped. Morning brings a heaviness that makes simple routines feel like obstacles. He used to get up early, make tea, and review the day’s organizing work before heading out. Now he sometimes remains in bed, staring at the ceiling, telling himself to get moving while another part of him resists the day. He feels more irritable than he used to and catches himself snapping at people over minor things. Afterwards he feels ashamed, as if the accident has made him less patient, less like the man he thought he was.

His work as a community organizer has become both anchor and burden. He still shows up to meetings, because the neighborhood depends on him and because idleness leaves too much room for memories. Yet he now enters crowded rooms with a wary edge, choosing seats near exits and watching doorways more than faces. Loud discussions can leave him abruptly tense, as though another collision might come at any moment. He finds it harder to concentrate during long conversations, and at times he loses his thread mid-sentence. He worries that people notice his distraction and will see him as diminished. This fear stings because his identity has long been tied to being useful, informed, and composed.

He also carries a persistent sense that his life divided into “before” and “after” the accident, and he mourns the version of himself that moved through the world without calculating every risk. At times he avoids talking about the event altogether, changing the subject when others ask how he is recovering. When memories intrude, they come with sensory force: the wet road, the metal crunch, the trapped feeling in his chest. He tries to push them away by keeping busy, but the effort leaves him drained. He describes feeling “on guard” much of the time, as if some part of him is always waiting for the next crash.

Despite this, he continues to care deeply about his community and about the people who rely on him. He still believes in showing up, even when the effort costs him. There are moments in session when he speaks with warmth about neighborhood victories and about the satisfaction of helping others. Yet beneath that commitment is a quieter life of fear, vigilance, and grief for the certainty he once had.
